titre: Oviraptor, the “Egg Thief” That Was Probably a Parent
accroche: Named in 1924 for a nest it supposedly raided, this Mongolian dinosaur was probably brooding: an embryo found in 1993 overturned the verdict.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1923, during the Central Asiatic Expeditions led by Roy Chapman Andrews in the Gobi Desert, in Mongolia, paleontologists from the American Museum of Natural History uncover the skeleton of a small beaked dinosaur, lying over a nest of elongated eggs. At this site, eggs of this type are then attributed to Protoceratops, a horned herbivore known from the same region. The scene seems easy to read: the predator was caught raiding a nest that was not its own.

## A Name That Passes Judgment

In 1924, Henry Fairfield Osborn names the animal Oviraptor philoceratops. The name translates as “egg seizer” or “egg thief,” with a “taste for ceratopsian eggs.” Osborn imagines that the animal died in a sandstorm in the middle of its theft. One detail is nonetheless in his material: the adult's skull is separated from the eggs by about ten centimeters of sediment. The verdict, for its part, sets in for decades.

## An Embryo Inside

In 1991, two researchers, Karol Sabath and Konstantine Mikhailov, challenge the association between Protoceratops and these elongated eggs. In 1993, a team from the American Museum, led by Mark Norell, finds at Ukhaa Tolgod, in Mongolia, an embryo skeleton in one of them. The embryo is that of a theropod dinosaur, not a ceratopsian. And the egg is identical in shape, size and texture to those that the 1923 expedition had found under the original adult. Norell and his colleagues publish it in Science in 1994: the adult was not a thief, but a parent brooding or guarding its clutch.

Other skeletons extend the argument. An adult discovered in 1993 in the same region rests crouched on a nest, arms stretched around the eggs, in a posture that the title of the article by James Clark, Mark Norell and Luis Chiappe (1999) compares to that of a brooding bird. This specimen would later be placed in a neighboring genus, Citipati, named in 2001, as was the embryo.

## What the Evidence Establishes

The chain of reasoning has to be read precisely. No one caught the original Oviraptor brooding: the fossil says nothing of its intention. The innocence rests on an identity between eggs, and on the fact that these eggs are those of a dinosaur of the oviraptorid family. The verdict is therefore probabilistic, but it is solid: an egg thief does not ordinarily settle on a nest, arms stretched around the eggs.

The name itself carries the lesson. Scientific nomenclature is not corrected when the interpretation changes: “egg thief” has remained attached to the animal even though the eggs have changed owners. A name thus keeps the trace of what was thought to be seen in 1924, long after science has stopped believing it. What remains to be known is how many other names carry, in the same way, a scene that no one has ever verified.

repere.texte: In 1993, an egg of the same type as those of the original nest, found at Ukhaa Tolgod (Mongolia), contains a theropod dinosaur embryo. The skull of the 1923 adult was separated from the eggs by ten centimeters of sediment.
repere.source: Norell et al., “A Theropod Dinosaur Embryo and the Affinities of the Flaming Cliffs Dinosaur Eggs,” Science, vol. 266, 1994, pp. 779-782

carte.punch: The 1924 “egg thief” was most likely a parent.
carte.idee: Named in 1924 for a nest it supposedly raided, Oviraptor was reexamined after a theropod embryo was found in 1993 in an egg identical to those of the nest. A scientific name can keep an error for a century.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Clark, Norell and Chiappe, “An oviraptorid skeleton from the late Cretaceous of Ukhaa Tolgod, Mongolia, preserved in an avianlike brooding position over an oviraptorid nest,” American Museum Novitates 3265, 1999
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The article that describes the skeleton crouched on its nest. Title and reference confirmed by the Embryo Project; the record page could not be opened from this environment.

quiz.question: What led Norell and his team to strip Oviraptor of its role as an egg thief?
choix: An analysis of the adult's fossilized stomach contents, with no eggshell
The redating of the 1923 skeleton, judged to be later than the laying of the nest
An egg identical to those of the original nest contained a theropod embryo
Tooth marks found on the nest's shells by the 1993 team
quiz.explication: The argument rests on the egg: the one from 1993, identical in shape, size and texture to those of the original nest, contained a theropod embryo, not a Protoceratops. No stomach contents, no redating and no tooth marks figure in this demonstration, which remains an inference and not a direct observation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who named the animal Oviraptor philoceratops, in 1924?
choix: Roy Chapman Andrews, who led the 1923 expedition
Mark Norell, who published the embryo study in 1994
Karol Sabath, who challenged the attribution of the eggs
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is Henry Fairfield Osborn who names the animal Oviraptor philoceratops in 1924, a name that translates as “egg thief fond of ceratopsians.”

quiz_supplementaire.question: What detail of the 1923 site already cast doubt on the idea of a theft caught in the act?
choix: The eggs bore tooth marks compatible with Protoceratops
The adult had been found several meters from the nest
The adult's skull was separated from the eggs by about ten centimeters of sediment
The eggs dated from a geological layer later than the skeleton
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The original adult's skull was separated from the eggs by about ten centimeters of sediment, a detail present from 1923 in Osborn's material but left without follow-up for decades.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What posture does the 1993 specimen, later placed in the genus Citipati, show?
choix: Standing over the nest, a broken egg in its mouth
Coiled around the nest like a snake protecting its clutch
Lying on its side, at a distance from the nest, without contact with the eggs
Crouched on the nest, arms stretched around the eggs, like a brooding bird
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1993 specimen, later assigned to the genus Citipati, is crouched on its nest with its arms stretched around the eggs, a posture compared to that of a bird brooding.
